authoredSolutions.1: In a parallel combination both capacitors share the same potential difference \(V\). From the charge-time graph the second capacitor settles at the larger charge, so \(q_{1} < q_{2}\). Since \(q = CV\) with \(V\) common, \(C_{1} < C_{2}\). The stored energy is \(U = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^{2}\), and with the same \(V\) this gives \(U_{1} < U_{2}\). Note also that at a common \(V\) the pairings \(C_{1} > C_{2}\) with \(U_{1} < U_{2}\), and \(C_{2} > C_{1}\) with \(U_{2} < U_{1}\), are internally impossible, so only two of the four options can even be considered. Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.2: For a ball falling through a viscous liquid the terminal velocity is \[v_{T} = \frac{2}{9}\frac{R^{2}g}{\eta}(d - \rho).\] Statement A: \(v_{T} \propto R^{2}\), so a plot of \(v_{T}\) against \(R\) is a parabola — true. Statement B: \(v_{T}\) depends on \(R^{2}\), so balls of different diameter have different terminal velocities — false. Statement C: \(\eta\) varies with temperature, so the measured terminal velocity is temperature dependent — true. Statement D: the liquid density \(\rho\) appears explicitly in the expression, so the experiment can be used to assess it — true. Statement E: the terminal velocity is the steady-state value at which net force vanishes and is independent of the launch speed, so \(\eta\) is unaffected — false. Only A, C and D hold, so the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.3: Statement A is stated the wrong way round: surface molecules possess the extra energy relative to interior molecules, which is the origin of surface tension — false. Statement B: for liquids the coefficient of viscosity decreases as temperature rises — false. Statement C: for gases viscosity arises from momentum transport by molecular motion, and \(\eta \propto \sqrt{T}\), so it increases with temperature — true. Statement D: the transition from laminar to turbulent flow is governed by the Reynolds number \(Re = \frac{\rho v D}{\eta}\) — true. Statement E: in steady flow the velocity at a point is unique, so two streamlines can never cross — true. Only C, D and E hold, so the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.4: For an infinite line charge of density \(\lambda\), the field at perpendicular distance \(r\) is \(E = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}\), so the potential is \[V = -\int E\,dr = -2k\lambda \ln r + \text{const}.\] The perpendicular distances of the point \((x,y,z)\) from the \(x\)-, \(y\)- and \(z\)-axes are \(\sqrt{y^{2}+z^{2}}\), \(\sqrt{z^{2}+x^{2}}\) and \(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\). Superposing, \[V = -2k\lambda\ln\!\left[\sqrt{(x^{2}+y^{2})(y^{2}+z^{2})(z^{2}+x^{2})}\right] + \text{const}.\] \(V\) is constant precisely when the product \((x^{2}+y^{2})(y^{2}+z^{2})(z^{2}+x^{2})\) is constant, so the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.5: Let the hemisphere have radius \(R\) with centre \(C\) at the middle of the flat top face; the coin sits at \(O\), the lowest point, a distance \(R\) below \(C\). The ray that can reach the observer at \(E\) leaves \(O\) and meets the curved surface at the rim point \(B\), which lies a distance \(R\) horizontally from \(C\). Taking \(C\) as origin, \(O = (0,-R)\) and \(B = (R,0)\), so the ray \(OB\) has direction \((R,R)\) while the normal at \(B\) is radial, along \((R,0)\). The angle of incidence inside the liquid is therefore \[i = 45^{\circ}.\] For the refracted ray to graze along \(BE\), the refraction angle must be \(90^{\circ}\): \[\mu \sin 45^{\circ} = \sin 90^{\circ} = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mu = \sqrt{2}.\] Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.6: Take the wire along \(z\) with current \(I\) in the \(+z\) direction, and let the particle be at distance \(x\) on the \(x\)-axis where \(\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi x}\hat{j}\). The equations of motion are \[m\frac{dv_{x}}{dt} = -qv_{z}B, \qquad m\frac{dv_{z}}{dt} = qv_{x}B = q\frac{dx}{dt}\frac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi x}.\] Integrating the second equation from \(x = a\), where \(v_{z} = v_{0}\), gives \[v_{z} = v_{0} + \frac{q\mu_{0}I}{2\pi m}\ln\!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right).\] The magnetic force does no work, so the speed stays \(v_{0}\); at the turning point \(v_{x} = 0\) and therefore \(v_{z} = -v_{0}\). Substituting, \[-v_{0} = v_{0} + \frac{q\mu_{0}I}{2\pi m}\ln\!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = a\,e^{-\frac{4\pi m v_{0}}{q\mu_{0}I}}.\] Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.7: For a Carnot engine \(\eta = 1 - \frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\). For the single engine \[\eta_{12} = 1 - \frac{273}{473} = \frac{200}{473} = 0.423.\] For the two staged engines \[\eta_{1} = 1 - \frac{373}{473} = \frac{100}{473} = 0.211, \qquad \eta_{2} = 1 - \frac{273}{373} = \frac{100}{373} = 0.268.\] Their sum is \(\eta_{1} + \eta_{2} = 0.479\), which exceeds \(\eta_{12} = 0.423\). (Algebraically, \(\eta_{1} + \eta_{2} = \eta_{12} + \eta_{1}\eta_{2} > \eta_{12}\).) Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.8: The speed of sound in a medium is \(v = \sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\). Although solids are far denser than gases, their bulk modulus is larger by a much greater factor, so sound indeed travels faster in solids — Assertion A is true. The Reason claims gases have a higher bulk modulus than solids, which is the opposite of the truth: solids are far less compressible and so have the much larger bulk modulus. Reason R is false. Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.9: From kinetic theory \[v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v_{rms}^{2} = \frac{3R}{M}T.\] The mean squared velocity is therefore directly proportional to the absolute temperature, so the graph is a straight line of positive slope passing through the origin, of the form \(y = mx\). The first option shows exactly this straight line through the origin, so the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.10: Measure angles from the lowest point of the hoop. A bead on the hoop at angle \(\theta\) from the bottom is joined to the bottom point by a chord of length \(2R\sin(\theta/2)\). Setting this equal to the natural length \(R\) gives \(\sin(\theta/2) = \tfrac{1}{2}\), i.e. \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\), so the bead is at height \(R(1 - \cos 60^{\circ}) = \tfrac{R}{2}\) above the bottom. Released from the top (height \(2R\)), the fall in height is \[\Delta h = 2R - \frac{R}{2} = \frac{3R}{2}.\] At the top the spring length is the diameter \(2R\), so its extension is \(2R - R = R\); at the final position the extension is zero. Energy conservation gives \[\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = mg\frac{3R}{2} + \frac{1}{2}kR^{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \sqrt{3gR + \frac{kR^{2}}{m}}.\] Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.11: A central force \(\vec{F} = F(r)\hat{r}\) gives \(\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = F(r)\,dr\), so the work integral depends only on the initial and final radii and not on the path. Assertion A is true. It is also true that not every force met in mechanics has an associated potential energy — friction and other dissipative forces are non-conservative — so Reason R is true. However R is a statement about non-conservative forces in general and does not explain why a central force is path-independent, so it is not the correct explanation. Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.12: The process is ordinary \(\beta^{-}\) decay of a free neutron. Charge conservation requires the products to carry net zero charge, which selects an electron rather than a positron. Lepton number conservation then requires the accompanying particle to be an antineutrino, since the electron carries lepton number \(+1\) and the neutron carries none: \[{}_{0}^{1}n \rightarrow {}_{1}^{1}p + {}_{-1}^{0}e + \bar{\nu}.\] Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.13: In the given circuit the upper AND gate receives \(A\) and \(\bar{B}\) (the inverter acts on \(B\)), while the lower AND gate receives \(A\) and \(B\). Their outputs feed a NOR gate: \[P = A\cdot\bar{B}, \qquad Q = A\cdot B,\] \[Y = \overline{P + Q} = \overline{A\bar{B} + AB} = \overline{A(B + \bar{B})} = \overline{A}.\] So the whole network is simply an inverter. The first option is a NAND gate with both inputs tied to \(A\), giving \(Y = \overline{A\cdot A} = \overline{A}\), the same output. Hence the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.14: Label the left terminal \(L\), the right terminal \(N\), and the two internal junctions \(P\) (between the first and second resistors) and \(Q\) (between the second and third resistors). Each resistor has value \(r/3\). The upper connecting wire shorts \(L\) to \(Q\), and the lower connecting wire shorts \(P\) to \(N\). Therefore \(L\) and \(Q\) are the same node, and \(P\) and \(N\) are the same node. Each of the three resistors then bridges these two nodes: the first joins \(L\) to \(P\), the second joins \(P\) to \(Q\), and the third joins \(Q\) to \(N\) — all three are in parallel between the two terminals. \[R_{eq} = \frac{r/3}{3} = \frac{r}{9}.\] Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.15: Since \(R = \frac{\rho \ell}{A}\), resistance is proportional to length for a wire of fixed cross-section. For the triangle each side is \(R/3\); across one edge that side is in parallel with the other two in series: \[R_{1} = \frac{\left(\frac{R}{3}\right)\left(\frac{2R}{3}\right)}{\frac{R}{3} + \frac{2R}{3}} = \frac{2R}{9}.\] For the square each side is \(R/4\); across one edge that side is in parallel with the other three in series: \[R_{2} = \frac{\left(\frac{R}{4}\right)\left(\frac{3R}{4}\right)}{\frac{R}{4} + \frac{3R}{4}} = \frac{3R}{16}.\] The required ratio is \[\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}} = \frac{2R/9}{3R/16} = \frac{32}{27}.\] Hence the correct choice is D.
authoredSolutions.16: The energy density of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the square of the electric field amplitude, \(u \propto E_{0}^{2}\). The energy held inside a cylinder of radius \(R\) and length \(L\) is therefore \[U \propto E_{0}^{2}\,\pi R^{2} L.\] Both cylinders have the same length and are to hold the same energy, so \[E_{1}^{2}R_{1}^{2} = E_{2}^{2}R_{2}^{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad E_{1}R_{1} = E_{2}R_{2}.\] The second cylinder has half the diameter, \(R_{2} = R_{1}/2\), giving \[E_{2} = 2E_{1} = 200\ \mathrm{NC^{-1}}.\] Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.17: The string keeps the charge at a fixed distance \(\ell\) from \(O\), so the particle swings on a circle of radius \(\ell\). Initially the string makes \(60^{\circ}\) with the \(x\)-axis, so the charge starts at \(x_{i} = \ell\cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{\ell}{2}\); when it crosses the \(x\)-axis it is at \(x_{f} = \ell\). The uniform field is along \(x\), so the work done by the electric force is \[W = qE(x_{f} - x_{i}) = qE\frac{\ell}{2}.\] The string tension is always perpendicular to the motion and does no work, so by the work-energy theorem \[\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{qE\ell}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \sqrt{\frac{qE\ell}{m}}.\] Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.18: Let the common energy be \(E\). For the photon \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\), so \[\lambda_{\text{photon}} = \frac{hc}{E}.\] For the non-relativistic proton \(E = \frac{p^{2}}{2m_{p}}\), so \(p = \sqrt{2m_{p}E}\) and \[\lambda_{\text{proton}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{p}E}}.\] The ratio is \[\frac{\lambda_{\text{proton}}}{\lambda_{\text{photon}}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_{p}E}}\cdot\frac{E}{hc} = \frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{E}{2m_{p}}}.\] Hence the correct choice is C.
authoredSolutions.19: Place the corner of the plate at the origin with the side \(a\) along \(x\) and \(b\) along \(y\). Since \(\sigma = \frac{\sigma_{0}x}{ab}\) does not depend on \(y\), the mass is distributed uniformly in the \(y\)-direction and \[y_{cm} = \frac{b}{2}.\] Taking a strip of width \(dx\) at position \(x\), \(dm = \sigma\,b\,dx = \frac{\sigma_{0}x}{a}dx\), so \[x_{cm} = \frac{\int_{0}^{a} x\,dm}{\int_{0}^{a} dm} = \frac{\int_{0}^{a} x^{2}dx}{\int_{0}^{a} x\,dx} = \frac{a^{3}/3}{a^{2}/2} = \frac{2a}{3}.\] The centre of mass is at \(\left(\frac{2a}{3}, \frac{b}{2}\right)\), so the correct choice is A.
authoredSolutions.20: For dispersion without deviation the net mean deviation of the combination must vanish, the two thin prisms being oppositely oriented: \[(\mu_{1} - 1)A_{1} = (\mu_{2} - 1)A_{2}.\] Substituting \(\mu_{1} = 1.54\), \(A_{1} = 4^{\circ}\) and \(\mu_{2} = 1.72\), \[(0.54)(4^{\circ}) = (0.72)A_{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad A_{2} = \frac{2.16}{0.72} = 3^{\circ}.\] Hence the correct choice is B.
authoredSolutions.21: The least count of the screw gauge is \[\text{L.C.} = \frac{\text{pitch}}{\text{number of circular scale divisions}} = \frac{0.75}{15} = 0.05\ \mathrm{mm}.\] This is the absolute uncertainty in each length measurement, so \(dL = dW = 0.05\ \mathrm{mm}\). For the area \(A = L\cdot W\) the fractional errors add: \[\frac{dA}{A} = \frac{dL}{L} + \frac{dW}{W} = \frac{0.05}{5} + \frac{0.05}{2.5} = \frac{1}{100} + \frac{2}{100} = \frac{3}{100}.\] Therefore \(x = 3\).
authoredSolutions.22: About a diameter, a disc has \(I = \frac{MR_{1}^{2}}{4}\) and a ring has \(I = \frac{MR_{2}^{2}}{2}\), the masses being equal. The given condition is \[\frac{MR_{1}^{2}/4}{MR_{2}^{2}/2} = 2.5 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{R_{1}^{2}}{2R_{2}^{2}} = \frac{5}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad R_{1}^{2} = 5R_{2}^{2}.\] A solid sphere of the same radius as the disc has \(I = \frac{2MR_{1}^{2}}{5}\) about a diameter, so \[n = \frac{2MR_{1}^{2}/5}{MR_{2}^{2}/2} = \frac{4R_{1}^{2}}{5R_{2}^{2}} = \frac{4(5R_{2}^{2})}{5R_{2}^{2}} = 4.\] Therefore \(n = 4\).
authoredSolutions.23: Modulus of elasticity is a stress, so \[[E] = \left[ML^{-1}T^{-2}\right],\] while torque has the dimensions of energy, \[[\tau] = \left[ML^{2}T^{-2}\right].\] The measured quantity is the ratio \[\frac{[E]}{[\tau]} = \frac{ML^{-1}T^{-2}}{ML^{2}T^{-2}} = \left[M^{0}L^{-3}T^{0}\right].\] Comparing with \(\left[M^{a}L^{b}T^{c}\right]\) gives \(a = 0\), \(b = -3\) and \(c = 0\). Therefore \(c = 0\).
authoredSolutions.24: Both discs are of the same material and of negligible (equal) thickness, so the mass is proportional to the face area: \(M \propto R^{2}\). About the central axis \[I = \frac{MR^{2}}{2} \propto R^{2}\cdot R^{2} = R^{4}.\] With \(R_{2} = 2R_{1}\), \[\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} = \left(\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}\right)^{4} = \frac{1}{16}.\] Comparing with \(1/x\) gives \(x = 16\).
authoredSolutions.25: In a double slit experiment the position of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) bright fringe is \[y_{n} = \frac{n\lambda D}{d}.\] Here \(n\), \(D\) and \(d\) are unchanged, so \(y \propto \lambda\): \[\frac{y_{2}}{y_{1}} = \frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad y_{2} = 10\ \mathrm{mm} \times \frac{660}{600} = 11\ \mathrm{mm}.\] Therefore the distance is \(11\) mm.
authoredSolutions.51: Since the number must exceed \(50000\), the first digit \(d_1\in\{5,6,7\}\); the last digit \(d_5\in\{0,\dots,7\}\) and the three middle digits are free, giving \(8^3=512\) choices each (repetition allowed). The constraint \(d_1+d_5\le 8\) gives: \(d_1=5\Rightarrow d_5\le3\) (4 values), \(d_1=6\Rightarrow d_5\le2\) (3 values), \(d_1=7\Rightarrow d_5\le1\) (2 values), i.e. \(9\) pairs. Count \(=9\times512=4608\). But this includes \(50000\) itself (\(d_1=5,d_5=0\)), which is not \(>50000\). Hence the answer is \(4608-1=4607.\)
authoredSolutions.52: Take points on \(y^2=4x\) as \((t^2,2t)\). With \(AD,BC\parallel y\)-axis, let \(A=(a^2,2a),\,D=(a^2,-2a),\,B=(b^2,2b),\,C=(b^2,-2b)\), so \(C\) has parameter \(-b\). Diagonal \(AC\) passes through the focus \((1,0)\), so it is a focal chord: \(a\cdot(-b)=-1\Rightarrow ab=1\). Its length is \((a^2+1)+(b^2+1)=a^2+b^2+2=\tfrac{25}{4}\Rightarrow a^2+b^2=\tfrac{17}{4}\). Then \((a+b)^2=\tfrac{25}{4}\) and \((a-b)^2=\tfrac{9}{4}\), so \(a+b=\tfrac52,\ |a-b|=\tfrac32\). The parallel sides are \(AD=4a,\ BC=4b\) with gap \(|a^2-b^2|\), so \[\text{Area}=\tfrac12(4a+4b)|a^2-b^2|=2(a+b)^2|a-b|=2\cdot\tfrac{25}{4}\cdot\tfrac32=\frac{75}{4}.\]
authoredSolutions.53: The powers of \(i\) cycle through \(\{i,-1,-i,1\}\) with equal probability \(\tfrac14\) each as \(k\) ranges over the naturals. The sum \(i^{k_1}+i^{k_2}=0\) exactly when \(i^{k_2}=-\,i^{k_1}\); for each of the \(4\) equally likely values of \(i^{k_1}\) there is precisely one such value of \(i^{k_2}\), giving \(P(\text{sum}=0)=\frac14\). Therefore \(P(\text{sum}\neq0)=1-\frac14=\frac{3}{4}.\)
authoredSolutions.54: For \(f(x)=\dfrac{2^{x}}{2^{x}+\sqrt2}\), compute \(f(1-x)\): multiplying numerator and denominator of \(\dfrac{2^{1-x}}{2^{1-x}+\sqrt2}\) by \(2^{x}\) gives \(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2^{x}+\sqrt2}\). In \(\sum_{k=1}^{81} f\!\left(\tfrac{k}{82}\right)\), pair \(k\) with \(82-k\): the \(40\) pairs \((1,81),\dots,(40,42)\) each sum to \(1\), and the middle term is \(f\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2\sqrt2}=\tfrac12\). authoredSolutions.55: Write \(f(x)=Ax^2+Bx+b\) with \(A=2+3a,\ B=\dfrac{a+2}{a-1}\). Expanding \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)+1-\tfrac27xy\) and matching the \(xy\) term gives \(2A=-\tfrac27\Rightarrow A=-\tfrac17\), so \(2+3a=-\tfrac17\Rightarrow a=-\tfrac57\); matching constants gives \(b=2b+1\Rightarrow b=-1\). authoredSolutions.56: Let \(A=(x,y,0)\). Equating distances to \((0,0,1)\) and \((0,3,2)\): \(y^2+1=(y-3)^2+4\Rightarrow y=2\); to \((0,0,1)\) and \((2,0,3)\): \(x^2+1=(x-2)^2+9\Rightarrow x=3\). Its area is \(\tfrac12\cdot AB\cdot AC=\dfrac92\neq\dfrac{9\sqrt2}{2}\), so \((S2)\) is false. Hence only \((S1)\) is true.
authoredSolutions.57: For \(R=\{(x,y):x,y\in Z,\ x+y\text{ even}\}\): (reflexive) \(x+x=2x\) is even, so \((x,x)\in R\). (symmetric) if \(x+y\) is even then \(y+x\) is even.
